steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a computer vision paper on weakly-supervised 3D human pose estimation from a single image using adversarial training with 2D-3D consistency. Cover the background and categories of methods, the weaknesses of reprojection-based approaches, our method, a contributions list, and a sentence on the evaluation datasets.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- 3D human pose estimation: importance and two categories of methods
- Limits of existing reprojection-based methods; depth ambiguity
- Our method: synchronized adversarial training with a reprojection network
- Discriminator design: 2D-3D consistency, random rotation, weighted KCS
- Contributions
- Experiments on public datasets

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Background
  - 3D pose from monocular images: long-standing problem in computer vision
  - applications: motion recognition, virtual reality, human-computer interaction
  - past three decades: dramatic increase in the field
  - end-to-end: image -> 3D pose directly with deep learning (cite)
  - two-stage: 2D joint coordinates from image (cite), then 3D from 2D (cite)
- Limits
  - many works focus on second stage, good performance, but ignore that a good 3D pose should reproject to plausible 2D pose
  - some recent methods use reprojection loss, better results (cite)
  - they train reprojection network by comparing 2D reprojection with input 2D poses (Figure 6 (a))
  - with detected 2D poses instead of ground truth -> big impact on reprojection accuracy
  - ignore: reasonable 3D pose should not collapse from a random viewing angle
  - fail on biggest challenge from single image: depth ambiguity
- Our method
  - weakly-supervised adversarial training, 2D-3D consistency, synchronous training of reprojection network (Figure 1)
  - train generator, reprojection network, discriminator together with GAN loss; reprojection net learns mapping of distribution 3D -> 2D
  - reduces influence of errors in generator input
  - generator: depth (z-component) from input 2D joints; rotate generated 3D pose; reprojection network reprojects rotated pose
- Discriminator
  - input: generated 3D pose + 2D reprojection -> 2D-3D consistency discrimination
  - with random rotation -> reduces depth ambiguity
  - inspired by original KCS matrix (cite): weight joint angle info between bones at different distances -> weighted kinematic chain space as third input; constrains bone lengths and joint angles
  - together: more accurate, interpretable results
- Contributions: novel adversarial network for 2D-3D consistency discrimination; synchronous strategy, mapping 2D->3D and inverse; improved wKCS
- Experiments: Human3.6M, MPI-INF-3DHP, MPII (cite each); outperforms weakly supervised SOTA; generalizes to unknown poses

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
3D human pose estimation from monocular images has always been a problem in computer vision. It can be used in many fields, like motion recognition, virtual reality, and human-computer interaction. In the past three decades the field of 3D human pose estimation has grown a lot. The various methods can be divided into two main categories. The first category is end-to-end methods, which process the image directly and estimate the 3D pose with a deep learning method. The second is two-stage methods, which first get the 2D joint coordinates from an image and then estimate the 3D pose from the 2D joint coordinates.

Many works focus on the second stage of the two-stage method and get good performance, but they often ignore the fact that a well-estimated 3D pose should be possible to reproject back to a plausible 2D pose. Recently some methods took the reprojection loss into account and got better results. But in these methods they trained the reprojection network by comparing the 2D reprojection with the input 2D poses, as shown in Figure 6 (a). This way of training has a big impact on the accuracy of the 2D reprojection when detected 2D poses are used as input instead of ground truth poses. Also these methods don't consider that a reasonable 3D pose should not collapse when you look at it from a random angle, in other words a high-quality 3D human pose estimate should look like a natural human body from any viewing angle. So they fail to deal effectively with the biggest challenge in 3D human pose estimation from a single image, which is the depth ambiguity problem.

- Our method: weakly-supervised adversarial training with 2D-3D consistency, synchronous training of reprojection network (Figure 1)
  - generator, reprojection network, discriminator trained together with GAN loss; reprojection network learns distribution mapping 3D -> 2D
  - reduces effect of errors in generator input
  - generator outputs depth (z-component) from 2D joints; rotate 3D pose; reprojection network reprojects it
- Discriminator: generated 3D pose + 2D reprojection -> 2D-3D consistency; plus random rotation -> less depth ambiguity
  - weighted KCS inspired by original KCS matrix; third input; bone lengths and joint angles
  - result: more accurate, interpretable
- Contributions (3 bullets)
- Datasets: Human3.6M, MPI-INF-3DHP, MPII; beats weakly supervised SOTA, generalizes to unknown poses

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
3D human pose estimation from monocular images has always been a problem in computer vision. It can be used in many fields, like motion recognition, virtual reality, and human-computer interaction. In the past three decades the field of 3D human pose estimation has grown a lot. The various methods can be divided into two main categories. The first category is end-to-end methods, which process the image directly and estimate the 3D pose with a deep learning method. The second is two-stage methods, which first get the 2D joint coordinates from an image and then estimate the 3D pose from the 2D joint coordinates.

Many works focus on the second stage of the two-stage method and get good performance, but they often ignore the fact that a well-estimated 3D pose should be possible to reproject back to a plausible 2D pose. Recently some methods took the reprojection loss into account and got better results. But in these methods they trained the reprojection network by comparing the 2D reprojection with the input 2D poses, as shown in Figure 6 (a). This way of training has a big impact on the accuracy of the 2D reprojection when detected 2D poses are used as input instead of ground truth poses. Also these methods don't consider that a reasonable 3D pose should not collapse when you look at it from a random angle, in other words a high-quality 3D human pose estimate should look like a natural human body from any viewing angle. So they fail to deal effectively with the biggest challenge in 3D human pose estimation from a single image, which is the depth ambiguity problem.

To solve these problems, in this paper we propose a weakly-supervised adversarial training method with 2D-3D consistency for estimating 3D human pose, and it uses a synchronous training strategy for training the reprojection network, as shown in Figure 1. In our model the generator, the reprojection network and the discriminator are trained synchronously with the loss function of the generative adversarial network, so that the reprojection network learns the mapping of the distribution from 3D poses to 2D poses. This training strategy can effectively reduce the influence of errors in the input of the generator. In our method, first we set up a generator that generates the depth (the z -component of the 3D coordinates) from the input 2D joint coordinates. Then we rotate the generated 3D pose and add a reprojection network to reproject the rotated 3D pose.

Finally we build a discriminator whose input contains a generated 3D pose and a 2D reprojection, and it performs 2D-3D consistency discrimination. When the 2D-3D consistency is combined with the random rotation of the generated 3D pose, our discrimination method can effectively reduce the depth ambiguity. Also, inspired by the original KCS matrix, we distinguish how important the joint angle information is between bones at different distances, and we propose to transform the 3D pose into a more elaborate weighted kinematic chain space, which is the third part of the discriminator's input, to put constraints on bone lengths and joint angles. With the synchronous training strategy, the random rotation discrimination, the 2D-3D consistency discrimination and the limits on bone lengths and joint angles, our model gets more accurate and interpretable estimation results. Our contributions are:

- We propose a new adversarial training network specifically for 2D-3D consistency discrimination, to improve the accuracy of 3D human pose estimation.

- We use a synchronous strategy to train the networks so they learn the mapping of the distribution from 2D poses to 3D poses and the inverse mapping, which can effectively reduce the influence of errors in the input 2D poses.

- We propose an elaborate improved kinematic chain space that transforms a 3D pose into a weighted kinematic chain space (wKCS) to put constraints on bone lengths and joint angles.

Experiments on three public datasets, Human3.6M, MPI-INF-3DHP, and MPII, show that our method is significantly better than state-of-the-art weakly supervised methods and can generalize to unknown 3D human poses.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
3D human pose estimation from monocular images has always been a problem in computer vision. It can be applied in multiple fields, such as motion recognition, virtual reality, and human-computer interaction. Over the past three decades, the field of 3D human pose estimation has grown dramatically. Existing methods can be divided into two main categories. One is the end-to-end method, which directly processes the image and estimates the 3D pose through a deep learning method [1,2,3,4,5,6]. The other is the two-stage method, which first obtains the 2D joint coordinates from an image [7,8,9,10,11,12,13] and then estimates the 3D pose from the 2D joint coordinates [14,15,16,17].

Although many works focus on the second stage of the two-stage method and achieve good performance, they often ignore the fact that a well-estimated 3D pose should be able to be reprojected back to a plausible 2D pose. Recently, some methods [18,17] have considered the reprojection loss and achieved better results. However, they trained the reprojection network by comparing the 2D reprojection with the input 2D poses, as shown in Figure 6 (a). This training strategy significantly affects the accuracy of the 2D reprojection when detected 2D poses are used as input instead of ground truth poses. These methods also do not consider that a reasonable 3D pose should not collapse when viewed at a random angle; that is, a high-quality 3D human pose estimate should look like a natural human body from any viewing angle. Hence they fail to effectively tackle the biggest challenge in 3D human pose estimation from a single image: the depth ambiguity problem.

To solve these problems, we propose in this paper a weakly-supervised adversarial training method with 2D-3D consistency to estimate a 3D human pose, which adopts a synchronous training strategy for the reprojection network, as shown in Figure 1. In our model, we synchronously train the generator, the reprojection network, and the discriminator using the loss function of the generative adversarial network, so that the reprojection network learns the mapping of the distribution from 3D poses to 2D poses. This training strategy effectively reduces the influence of errors in the input of the generator. In our method, we first set up a generator to generate the depth (the z -component of the 3D coordinates) from the input 2D joint coordinates. We then rotate the generated 3D pose and add a reprojection network to reproject the rotated 3D pose.

Finally, we construct a discriminator, whose input contains a generated 3D pose and a 2D reprojection, to perform 2D-3D consistency discrimination. By combining the 2D-3D consistency with the random rotation of the generated 3D pose, our discrimination method effectively reduces the depth ambiguity. Moreover, inspired by the original KCS matrix [17], we distinguish the importance of the joint angle information between bones at different distances, and propose to transform the 3D pose into a more elaborate weighted kinematic chain space that serves as the third part of the discriminator’s input, imposing constraints on bone lengths and joint angles. Using the synchronous training strategy, random rotation discrimination, 2D-3D consistency discrimination and the constraints on bone lengths and joint angles, our model obtains more accurate and interpretable estimation results. Our contributions are as follows:

- • We propose a novel adversarial training network specifically for 2D-3D consistency discrimination, to improve the accuracy of 3D human pose estimation.

- • We employ a synchronous strategy to train the networks to learn the mapping of the distribution from 2D poses to 3D poses and the inverse mapping, which effectively reduces the influence of errors in the input 2D poses.

- • We propose an elaborate improved kinematic chain space that transforms a 3D pose into a weighted kinematic chain space (wKCS) to impose constraints on bone lengths and joint angles.

Experimental results on three public datasets, Human3.6M [19], MPI-INF-3DHP [20], and MPII [21], show that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art weakly supervised methods and generalizes to unknown 3D human poses.
